      <title>US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/26/us-forces-accused-of-weaponising-somalia-flood-el-nino</link>
      <description><p><strong>Exclusive:</strong> Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river where rising water levels are a threat to safety. Is it a deliberate military strategy?</p><p>The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.</p><p>“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/26/us-forces-accused-of-weaponising-somalia-flood-el-nino">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Reader Q&A: After Lula’s sensational victory in Brazil’s presidential election, the Guardian’s Latin America correspondent answers your questions</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2026/oct/27/brazil-election-reader-questions-lula-bolsonaro</link>
      <description><p>Having lost the first round of Brazil’s presidential election to far right rival Flávio Bolsonaro, incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spectacularly triumphed in the second. What comes next for Brazil? The Guardian’s Tom Phillips is answering your questions now.</p><p><strong>Ask a question: log in or sign up </strong><a href="https://profile.theguardian.com/signin"><strong>here</strong></a><strong> to comment, or email conversations@theguardian.com</strong></p><p><strong>Jeremy Hurley asks: </strong>Why did the Brazil stock market tank after the election result, and will it recover?</p><p><strong>Tom: </strong>Basically, because the markets had been convinced that Flávio Bolsonaro was going to win and that after taking power he would implement a “chainsaw” style austerity programme inspired by Javier Milei’s government in Argentina, deal with Brazil’s budget deficit, and bring down interest rates. Lula’s victory came as a shock to investors who believe his fourth presidency will see increased and unsustainable public spending.</p><p>Yes, I’m sure things will stabilise at some point soon after the initial panic – during Lula’s previous administrations investors made a lot of money, particularly during his first two terms. There is talk of Lula naming his vice-president, the centre-right politician Geraldo Alckmin, as finance minister in order to calm markets down. Another possible name Rafael Fonteles, a mathematician who is the governor of Piauí and used to run that state’s finances.</p><p><strong>Tom: </strong>Hi Adam. That’s a really good question and, as someone who lives in Rio de Janeiro, it is one that has been on my mind a lot. The far right has been very good at blaming “soft” left wing policies and federal government incompetence for the failure to control armed violence. It was a huge part of the campaign against Lula in the run up to this election.</p><p>But public security is a state matter and Rio state has largely been governed by the right for years now. Their hard-line, shoot first ask questions later approach has not worked - in fact many believe it has made the violence even worse and led to massacres such as the one I covered in the Complexo da Penha almost exactly one year ago. It must be said that similar tactics have been used in Bahia state, which has a huge problem with violence and is governed by the Worker’s party (PT). My colleague Tiago Rogero has <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/article/2024/aug/14/bahia-brazil-police-killings-rate">written about this</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2026/oct/27/brazil-election-reader-questions-lula-bolsonaro">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/politics/live/2026/oct/27/budget-burnham-healey-everday-fixes-gherkins-conservatives-miliband-carers-latest-news-updates</link>
      <description><p>Greens say Labour has ‘no respect for young people’ amid reports chancellor will pause equalisation of minimum wage for under-21s with that paid to older workers</p><p><strong>Jonathan Reynolds</strong>, the business secretary, has not contested reports saying that, in the budget tomorrow, John Healey, the chancellor, will pause the process of equalising the lower national minimum wage paid to people under the age of 21 with the more generous national living wage that applies to older workers.</p><p>In an interview on the BBC this morning, Reynolds was asked to respond to a story suggesting the equalisation process has been put on hold because of concerns about youth unemployment.</p><p>John Healey will announce plans to increase the minimum wage by nearly 4% but slow the rise for young people after warnings that they are being priced out of jobs.</p><p>The Times has been told that the national living wage, which applies to those aged 21 and over, is expected to rise from £12.71 to around £13.20 – an increase of 3.9%.</p><p>The manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies, but it was always clear it would happen over time and we would take into account, as the minimum wage uprating each year always does, the relative strength of the labour market and other pressures …</p><p>Of course, you want not just good wages, but good work. And the way this has always been done – it is a balance of making sure the pressures on the labour market are taken into account. That is the approach you will see confirmed [in the budget].</p><p>Anyone doing a day’s work, needs to be paid the same rate for the same job. A young person’s rent and food bill is no less because they are young, so they need to receive the same wage.</p><p>Healey and Burnham are now breaking a manifesto pledge to young people that even Starmer managed to keep. Labour have no respect for young people, who appear to just be there for cheap labour for the wealthy and their corporate donors.</p><p>[It] wouldn’t be my cup of tea, but I wouldn’t ban anybody from doing so … I don’t want us to get into a world of cancel culture.</p><p>I’m not going to have run a party where we say you can’t talk about that person or that person. We have to be sensible about vetting. And we are.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/politics/live/2026/oct/27/budget-burnham-healey-everday-fixes-gherkins-conservatives-miliband-carers-latest-news-updates">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>First Thing: Trump targets midterm legitimacy with lawsuits and a cash bounty</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/27/first-thing-trump-targets-midterm-legitimacy-with-lawsuits-and-a-cash-bounty</link>
      <description><p>US president in unprecedented offer of $1m reward for reports of voter fraud as DoJ acts against states. Plus, everything you need to know about Israel’s crucial election</p><p>Good morning. The Trump administration’s assault on the legitimacy of the midterm elections has continued, with the US president <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/26/trump-reward-reporting-voter-fraud">announcing a $1m reward</a> for reports of voter fraud, amid several legal actions by the Department of Justice to limit voting.</p><p>Donald Trump said the bounty payment was contingent on the arrest and conviction of those responsible. He did not disclose how he would pay for the rewards. Trump’s comments follow his repeated and unfounded claims of widespread voter fraud.</p><p><strong>What action is the administration trying to take against Washington state?</strong> The administration has asked Washington state <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/26/trump-washington-ballots-aside-noncitizen-voters">to set aside</a> any ballots received from more than 400 people it alleges are registered to vote without US citizenship. The request marks the third time this month that the justice department has brought a direct state challenge even as voting is under way.</p><p><strong>What is the latest in the battle over California voters?</strong> A US federal appeals court has <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/26/court-california-ballots">rejected the Trump administration’s move</a> to block California from counting the ballots of 20,000 registered voters that the justice department claims are non-citizens.</p><p><strong>Why is </strong><strong>Vivek Ramaswamy</strong><strong> facing criticism </strong><strong>over an advert?</strong> The Republican nominee to be the governor of Ohio ran an ad featuring his opponent’s mother, who said she would not vote for her daughter. As Moira Donegan explains in <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/27/vivek-ramaswamy-ad-midterms-opinion">this excoriating opinion piece</a>, the estrangement between Amy Acton is decades long and stems from the sexual abuse Acton survived as a child.</p><p><strong>What are the key takeaways from the investor prospectus?</strong> The document reveals the AI research lab’s financials and the risks – more than 90 pages of them – that might negatively impact its business. Johana Bhuiyan has identified <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/26/anthropic-stock-market-filing-takeaways">these four key takeaways</a>.</p><p><strong>What has Anthropic’s model recently been accused of?</strong> Anthropic’s Claude model <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/26/anthropics-claude-ai-model-accessed-georgia-voter-data-in-us">accessed voter data in the US state of Georgia</a>, the AI company has confirmed, in the latest example of unauthorised behavior by the technology. The AI model managed to bypass a paywall to reach data that is publicly available but is typically accessible only after paying a fee.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/27/first-thing-trump-targets-midterm-legitimacy-with-lawsuits-and-a-cash-bounty">Continue reading...</a></description>
